title: A real smart home means more than collecting remote controls
description: Imagine owning a company with 20 talented employees, each doing their own job well, but no manager, coordinator, or overall direction. Would it operate efficiently? body:
Imagine you own a company.

You have 20 talented employees.

Everyone is capable and does their own job well.

But there is no manager,

no coordinator,

and nobody looking at the overall picture.

Everyone works independently.

Would that company operate efficiently?

Many smart homes are like this.

Homeowners invest in

• Smart bulbs

• Motorized curtains

• Smart air conditioning

• CCTV cameras

• Digital Door Lock

• Smart Plug

• Voice-controlled speakers

• Sensors

Their phones end up full of applications.

They must open several apps,

control each device separately,

and remember how different systems work.

A smart home should make life easier,

rather than more complicated.

Many people assume that

owning many smart devices

means having a smart home.

In reality,

these are simply smart devices.

They do not yet form a smart home.

A true smart home

lets all its devices work together automatically.

For example,

when you drive home,

the gate opens automatically,

pathway lights switch on,

air conditioning starts,

security changes to Home mode,

and curtains open or close on schedule.

All this happens without picking up your phone.

That is the difference between

a home with smart devices

and

a true smart home.

The number of devices is not what matters.

What matters is designing a system in which everything works together intelligently.

Technology should look after the home,

so the homeowner does not have to look after the technology.

title: Why is your home Wi-Fi slow despite an expensive internet plan?
description: Do you pay for 500 Mbps or 1,000 Mbps internet but still face connection problems? Speed may not be the issue; Wi-Fi distribution within the building may be. Strong internet is like a strong water supply: narrow, blocked, or poorly routed pipes still restrict flow. Poor router positioning, insufficient access points, substandard LAN cables, and unsuitable network design can make even fast internet unstable. Good Wi-Fi begins with assessing the space, positioning access points, installing suitable LAN cabling, and planning reliable infrastructure…
body:
Have you experienced this?

You pay for high-speed internet every month,

with a 500 Mbps or 1,000 Mbps package,

yet the same problems keep occurring:

  • YouTube freezes,
  • Zoom meetings disconnect,
  • gaming latency is high,
  • the bedroom signal is weak,
  • the second floor has no usable connection,
  • or Wi-Fi drops when you move across the house.

Many people think
“My internet is not fast enough.”

But internet speed may not be the cause.

The issue may be Wi-Fi distribution within the home or building.

Fast internet is like a strong mains water supply.

If household pipes are too narrow, poorly routed, or blocked,
water still will not flow well.

Wi-Fi works similarly.

Even with a high-speed internet package,
a poorly positioned router,
too few access points,

substandard LAN cabling,
or unsuitable network design

can leave the connection unstable.

Good Wi-Fi requires more than an expensive router.

It starts with a design suited to the actual space, including:

✓ Assessing the home or building size

✓ Designing stable network infrastructure

✓ Reducing dead zones and signal interference

✓ Supporting multiple simultaneous users

✓ Maintaining reliable long-term operation

Why Is Your Wi-Fi Still Slow Even Though You Pay for High-Speed Internet?

Have you ever subscribed to a 500 Mbps or even 1 Gbps internet plan, only to find that your Wi-Fi still feels slow?

You are not alone.

Many homeowners and business owners experience the same frustration every day.

  • Netflix keeps buffering
  • Video calls freeze during important meetings
  • Online games suffer from high latency
  • Wi-Fi works in one room but not another
  • The second floor has weak signal coverage
  • Smart home devices randomly disconnect

Most people assume the problem is their internet provider.

But in many cases, the internet speed is not the real issue.

The real problem is the Wi-Fi system itself.

Think of it this way.

High-speed internet is like water pressure coming into your house.

You may have strong water pressure from the main supply, but if the pipes inside your home are too small, poorly installed, or routed incorrectly, the water will never flow efficiently.

Wi-Fi works exactly the same way.

Even with a fast internet package, poor network design can prevent you from getting the performance you are paying for.

Common causes include:

  • Poor router placement
  • Insufficient access points
  • Weak Wi-Fi coverage
  • Outdated network equipment
  • Poor quality LAN cabling
  • Network congestion and interference

A reliable Wi-Fi network is not built by simply buying the most expensive router.

It requires proper planning and professional network design.

A well-designed Wi-Fi and network infrastructure should include:

✓ Site survey and coverage analysis

✓ Strategic Access Point placement

✓ Professional LAN cabling

✓ Stable network infrastructure

✓ Elimination of Wi-Fi dead zones

✓ Seamless roaming between areas

✓ Support for multiple users and devices

✓ Scalability for future expansion

At AITS, we believe Wi-Fi is no longer just about internet access.

Today, Wi-Fi supports almost every critical technology system in a home or business, including:

• CCTV Systems

• Smart Home Automation

• IoT Devices

• Access Control Systems

• Enterprise Applications

• Video Conferencing

• Cloud Services

• Business Operations

When the network becomes unstable, everything connected to it can be affected.

That is why investing in proper network infrastructure is just as important as investing in fast internet service.

Before upgrading your internet package again, ask yourself:

“Is my network designed correctly?”

Because fast internet alone does not guarantee a great user experience.

The true foundation of a reliable digital lifestyle is a properly designed Wi-Fi and network infrastructure system.

At AITS, we specialize in designing and implementing professional Wi-Fi, LAN, and network infrastructure solutions for homes, offices, retail spaces, warehouses, factories, and commercial projects.

Our goal is simple:

To ensure every device, every system, and every user stays connected—reliably, securely, and efficiently.

Much like insurance, you may not think about it every day.

But when an incident happens, it suddenly becomes one of the most valuable investments you have ever made.

Whether it is:

• An accident inside a home, office, or commercial property

• Property damage, theft, or vandalism

The first question is almost always the same:

“Can we review the CCTV footage?”

Unfortunately, this is also the moment when many security systems fail.

Common issues include:

• CCTV cameras not recording

• Video footage that is too blurry to identify individuals

• Failed hard drives and storage systems

• CCTV systems shutting down during power outages

• Poor camera placement creating critical blind spots

• Network infrastructure failures preventing footage retrieval

The problem is often not the CCTV camera itself.

Raise pool villas and resorts to a new standard with smart systems by AITS

Thailand’s villa and resort industry increasingly competes on the guest experience, beyond price alone.

Today’s guests expect more than a comfortable bed or a beautiful view.

They want a high level of convenience, security and privacy.

This is where smart automation plays an important role.

AITS designs Smart Villa and Smart Resort systems around

guest experience, operations, security and energy cost control.

A better guest experience

Imagine guests arriving at a villa.

The gate opens automatically as their registered vehicle approaches.

Pathway and pool lights turn on to welcome them.

The indoor air conditioning is set to the desired temperature in advance.

Music switches to a gentle welcome setting.

Guests do not need to contact staff,

collect a key

or configure any systems.

Everything is designed to be ready to use immediately.

This is the difference between ordinary accommodation and a professionally designed Smart Villa.

SystemKeyless access and automated check-in management

AITS integrates smart door locks and access control with the management system.

Passcodes or digital keys can be valid only during the booked stay.

When the booking ends, access is revoked automatically.

This reduces the risk of lost keys,

reduces staff workload

and improves security.

Security that does not disturb guests

A Smart Resort needs to be safe without making guests feel watched.

AITS designs camera zones and AI CCTV systems to focus on public areas.

They detect unusual events, such as outsiders entering restricted areas or unusual movement late at night.

The system can alert the manager immediately, without requiring someone to watch a screen all day.

Proactive security, rather than waiting for an incident

Intelligent energy cost control

Electricity is one of a resort’s main operating costs.

AITS installs Smart Energy Monitoring systems that can:

• Detect unoccupied rooms where air conditioners have been left running

• Activate energy-saving mode automatically when there are no guests

• Analyze peak usage periods

• Present management reports in a dashboard

The result is lower long-term costs without compromising the guest experience.

Centralized management

For owners of multiple villas or buildings,

AITS can bring all systems into a single central dashboard.

Management can:

• Check the status of every room

• View camera footage in real time

• Control lighting and air conditioning

• Check alarms and event logs

Whether in Bangkok, Phuket or Chiang Mai,

all locations are available on one screen.

Smart Villa & Resort Automation

Elevating Hospitality Standards with Intelligent Systems by AITS

The villa and resort market in Thailand is no longer competing on price alone.

Today, the real differentiator is guest experience.

Modern travelers expect more than beautiful views and comfortable beds.

They expect convenience, security, privacy, and seamless technology.

This is where intelligent automation becomes a strategic advantage.

AITS designs Smart Villa and Smart Resort systems by integrating four critical dimensions:

Guest experience.

Operational efficiency.

Advanced security.

Energy cost optimization.

A Seamless Guest Experience from the Moment of Arrival

Imagine a guest arriving at a private villa.

The registered vehicle approaches, and the gate opens automatically.

Pathway and pool lighting activate softly.

Indoor air conditioning has already adjusted to a comfortable temperature.

Ambient welcome lighting sets the mood.

There is no need for key handover.

No manual setup.

No waiting for staff.

Everything is prepared in advance.

This is the difference between a standard rental property and a professionally engineered Smart Villa.

Keyless Access & Automated Check-In Management

AITS integrates smart door locks and access control systems directly with booking management logic.

Temporary digital keys can be issued for specific stay periods.

Once the booking ends, access is automatically revoked.

This approach:

Enhances security.

Eliminates lost key risks.

Reduces staff workload.

Improves operational control.

Intelligent Security Without Disturbing Guests

A smart resort must be secure — without making guests feel monitored.

AITS designs AI CCTV zoning strategies that prioritize:

Public and perimeter areas.

Restricted staff zones.

Unauthorized access detection.

Night-time anomaly detection.

Managers receive intelligent alerts instead of reviewing footage continuously.

This is proactive security, not reactive monitoring.

Intelligent Energy Cost Management

Energy consumption is one of the largest operating expenses for villas and resorts.

AITS implements Smart Energy Monitoring systems capable of:

Detecting rooms with air conditioning left running without occupancy.

Automatically activating energy-saving mode when guests check out.

Analyzing peak consumption patterns.

Providing centralized reporting dashboards for management.

The result is reduced operational cost without compromising guest comfort.

Centralized Multi-Property Management

For owners operating multiple villas or properties, AITS provides centralized control systems.

From a single dashboard, management can:

Monitor property status in real time.

View CCTV across all locations.

Control lighting and HVAC remotely.

Track alarms and system events.

Access historical analytics.

Whether located in Bangkok, Phuket, or Chiang Mai, the entire portfolio remains under one secure system.

Concept Comparison

Traditional Resort Model:

Physical keys.

Manual energy management.

Basic CCTV recording.

Independent subsystems.

Limited operational visibility.

AITS Smart Villa & Resort Model:

Digital keyless access.

Automated guest experience scenarios.

AI-driven security alerts.

Smart energy optimization.

Centralized enterprise-level management.

AITS does not install isolated smart devices.

We engineer intelligent hospitality ecosystems.

We integrate:

Enterprise-grade network infrastructure.

AI-powered security systems.

Automation aligned with the guest journey.

Energy optimization strategies.

A truly smart resort is not just modern.

body:
A comprehensive AITS guide for detached houses, condominiums and villas

Searches for “How much does smart home installation cost?” and

“What do I need to prepare for a smart home?”

are steadily increasing in Thailand.

But the important question is:

How do you install a system that is stable, secure and ready for the future?

This is the guide AITS uses when designing systems.

Step1: Plan the system infrastructure before choosing devices

A common mistake is

choosing devices before planning the network architecture.

A good smart home begins with:

• Separating the IoT network with a VLAN

• Plan access point locations

• Calculate bandwidth requirements for AI CCTV

• Provide UPS backup power

With poor infrastructure,

even the best devices cannot operate reliably.

Step2: Choose a wired, wireless or hybrid system

Wireless systems

Suit homes that have already been built.

They are easy to install, but require careful control of Wi-Fi quality.

Wired systems, such as KNX / RS485

Offer high stability and suit new or luxury homes.

Hybrid systems, a common choice in AITS designs

Combine the advantages of both approaches,

adding flexibility and supporting future expansion.

Step3: Design automation around real behavior

Do not start the design with features.

Start with your lifestyle.

Examples:

• Wake-up times

• Working hours

• Lighting usage habits

• Security requirements

AITS uses behavior-based automation,

beyond time-based automation alone.

Step4: Integrate security with the smart home

A complete smart home must connect to:

• AI CCTV

• Smart Door Lock

• Alarm System

• Access Control

Systems must work together as an integrated whole.

Step5: Prepare for future expansion

A smart home in 2026 needs to support:

• AI Integration

• Energy Monitoring

• Solar Integration

• EV Charger Management

• Cloud + Local Hybrid Processing

Homes should be designed to be ready for upgrades.

What is the starting budget?

The budget depends on the size of the home and the system level.

Typical levels include:

• Entry level: lighting and app control

• Mid-range: automation and AI CCTV integration

• Advanced: Deep AI, enterprise networking and full security integration

AITS assesses the actual space and the customer’s requirements.

Why choose AITS

AITS provides more than individual devices.

We design complete, integrated systems.

Our expertise includes:

• Network Infrastructure

• AI CCTV

• Automation Design

• Energy Optimization

• Enterprise Security Architecture

A good smart home

starts with sound engineering.

How to Install a Smart Home in Thailand (2026 Guide)

A Complete Installation Framework by AITS

Searches such as “How much does Smart Home installation cost?” and

“What is required to build a smart home?” are increasing rapidly in Thailand.

But the real question is:

How do you design a system that is stable, secure, and future-ready?

This is the same framework AITS uses when engineering Smart Home systems for houses, condominiums, and luxury villas.

Step 1: Design the Infrastructure Before Choosing Devices

One of the most common mistakes is selecting devices before designing the network architecture.

A reliable smart home must begin with:

• VLAN segmentation for IoT network isolation

• Proper WiFi access point planning

• Bandwidth calculation for AI CCTV systems

• UPS backup design

Without strong infrastructure, even premium devices will fail to deliver stability.

Step 2: Choose Between Wired, Wireless, or Hybrid Systems

Wireless Systems

Ideal for completed homes.

Quick installation but requires carefully optimized WiFi infrastructure.

Wired Systems (e.g., KNX / RS485)

Highly stable and suitable for new builds or luxury homes.

Hybrid Systems (Preferred by AITS)

Combines wired stability with wireless flexibility.

Provides scalability and long-term upgrade potential.

Step 3: Design Automation Based on Lifestyle, Not Features

Do not design automation based on functions.

Design it around real-life behavior.

Consider:

• Wake-up routines

• Work schedules

• Lighting habits

• Security preferences

AITS implements behavior-based automation, not just time-based scheduling.

Step 4: Integrate Security Into the Smart Home Ecosystem

A true smart home integrates with:

• AI CCTV systems

• Smart door locks

• Alarm systems

• Access control

All systems must work together — not operate independently.

Step 5: Build for Future Expansion

A 2026 smart home should be ready for:

• AI integration

• Energy monitoring

• Solar system integration

• EV charger management

• Hybrid cloud + local processing

Homes should be designed to support upgrades — not require full redesign later.

Budget Considerations

Budget depends on property size and system complexity.

Typical tiers include:

• Entry-level: Lighting + mobile app control

• Mid-level: Automation + AI CCTV integration

• Advanced level: Deep AI learning + enterprise network + full security integration

AITS evaluates each project based on actual space usage and client requirements.

Why Choose AITS

AITS does not sell isolated devices.

We engineer complete smart ecosystems.

Our expertise includes:

• Enterprise network infrastructure

• AI CCTV integration

• Automation system design

• Energy optimization

• Advanced security architecture

Because a true smart home must begin with proper engineering.

When your home can truly learn your habits

Traditional smart homes operate according to commands.

Advanced smart homes operate according to behavior.

This is the difference between conventional automation and

AITS Deep AI Behavior Learning Architecture

a home that does more than respond to commands:

it learns, analyzes and adapts to the homeowner’s lifestyle.

What does Deep AI mean in a smart home?

Deep AI in an AITS system combines:

• AI CCTV Analytics

• Sensor Data Aggregation

• User Behavior Pattern Modeling

• Machine-Learning Based Automation Logic

The system does more than follow fixed schedules.

It learns from actual data, such as:

• Arrival and departure times

• Frequently used rooms

• Your usual temperature settings

• Lighting usage habits

• Movement during the night

ArchitectureDeep AI Architecture by AITS

1. Data Collection Layer

Data is collected from:

• AI Camera (Face / Movement / Vehicle Detection)

• PIR & Motion Sensor

• Door/Window Contact Sensor

• Temperature & Humidity Sensor

• Smart Energy Meter

• Mobile GPS Presence

All data is processed using a local-first approach to reduce latency and improve security.

2. Pattern Recognition Engine

The system analyzes behavior, such as:

• The homeowner regularly arrives home between 18:30 and 19:00

• The study lights are on between 21:00 and 23:00

• The air conditioner is set to 24°C almost every day

• There is no movement downstairs after midnight

Once a clear pattern emerges, the system starts anticipating needs.

3. Predictive Automation Layer

Using what it has learned, the system can:

• Turn on lights before you enter a room

• Adjust air conditioning to your preferred temperature without a command

• Automatically switch off unused zones

• Alert you to activity that differs from normal patterns

This is behavior-based automation, beyond time-based automation.

A practical example

Normal situation:

The homeowner arrives at 19:00.

The system turns on the lights and air conditioning automatically.

Unusual situation:

One day, movement is detected in the kitchen at 03:00,

outside the usual pattern.

the system will:

• Send an immediate alert

• Turn on floodlights

• Record the event as high risk

This analyzes anomalies against actual behavior patterns.

Benefits in depth

AITS Deep AI Smart Home helps:

• Reduce energy use without manual configuration

• Reduce false alarms

• Improve predictive security

• Increase convenience without repeated commands

body:
Deep Analytics & Intelligent Security by AITS

In the past, the main purpose of CCTV was to record footage for later review.

In the AI era, cameras need to do more.

Modern AI CCTV goes beyond recording

to become a real-time decision system.

This is what distinguishes the systems AITS designs.

System architecture AITS AI CCTV Architecture

1. Edge AI Camera (Deep Learning Processor)

AI cameras with onboard processing chips can:

• Analyze faces using face recognition

• Detect people and vehicles

• Distinguish household members from unfamiliar people

• Detect intrusions

• Line Crossing Detection

• Perimeter Protection

Processing at the camera reduces server workload and latency.

2. AI NVR with Intelligent Analytics

An AITS NVR does more than record footage.

It can:

• Group events by type, such as people or vehicles

• Search recorded footage by face

• Filter false alarms caused by animals or lighting

• Create an event timeline for analysis

This can make finding evidence several times faster.

3. Behavior-Based Alert System

The system does not alert you to every movement.

It alerts you to important events only.

Examples:

• An unfamiliar person enters the backyard at 02:00

• An unregistered vehicle enters the property

• Unusual loitering occurs near the fence

This is an intelligent alert, beyond a basic motion alert.

Comparing the approaches

Conventional CCTV:

• Only records footage

• Alerts on every movement

• Requires manual review to find recorded events

• Does not analyze behavior

AITS AI CCTV:

• Analyzes footage in real time

• Alerts only on unusual events

• Searches using face recognition

• Provides event analytics

• Reduce false alarms

Integration with smart homes and mobile devices

AITS AI CCTV systems can connect to:

• Smart Alarm System

• Smart Lighting

• Access Control

• Mobile App Dashboard

Examples:

When a camera detects an unfamiliar person in a restricted zone,

The system can:

• Turn on floodlights

• Send a notification with a snapshot

• Record the event as a highlight

• Activate a siren automatically

All of this happens within seconds.

Enterprise-level security for homes

AITS brings enterprise security standards to residential properties.

• Network Segmentation

• Secure Data Storage

• Role-Based Access Control

• Remote Secure Monitoring

• Backup Redundancy

Home security should meet the same standards as enterprise security.

Why choose AITS

AITS provides more than camera installation.

We design intelligent security systems.

Our expertise includes:

• Network Infrastructure

• AI Deep Learning System

• CCTV Enterprise Design

• Automation Integration

Good cameras alone are not enough.

The system must analyze, decide and respond.

One problem many organizations face isa disorganized internal network, with unidentified cable endpoints and equipment without names or tags.


This makes maintenance and troubleshooting time-consuming and increases the risk of system interruptions.

AITS therefore offersnetwork organization and tagging for every device to enterprise standards,helping customer networks become

The AITS Professional Network Organizing Process

1. Inspect the existing infrastructure: Network Audit & Mapping

AITS collects information at every point, including:

  • Which VLANs each switch uses
  • Which devices connect to each port
  • LAN and fiber cable routes
  • Unused ports and devices
  • Areas at risk of short circuits or damage

The result is anetwork diagram and asset listcovering every device.

2. Reorganize all LAN and fiber cables: Cable Management

The AITS team follows standard practices:

  • Rebundle cables with Velcro, avoiding plastic ties that can damage them
  • Align cables neatly along vertical and horizontal routes
  • Keep cable runs as short as appropriate to reduce interference
  • Use patch panels with clearly ordered, readable port layouts

The result isa thoroughly organized, professional rack cabinet.

3. Tag every device: AITS Device Tagging Standard

Each device tag includes:

  • Device name
  • IP address
  • Switch port number
  • Patch panel number
  • Cable source and destination
  • Installation date and responsible team

Waterproof, dust-resistant tags with a service life of 3–5 years

Example tags used by AITS:
AC-01 / SW-02 / AP-L3 / CAM-FRONT-01

4. Label every cable to a consistent standard: Professional Cable Labeling

We use heat-resistant, dust-resistant labels suited to office buildings and factories.
Every cable has a clear identifier, helping to

  • resolve problems 3–5 times faster,
  • avoid tracing cables again each time
  • and prevent accidental disconnection.

5. Update all network documentation: Documentation & Handover

Customers receive:

  • Network Diagram
  • Port Mapping Sheet
  • IP Addressing Scheme
  • A complete equipment asset list
  • A basic system maintenance guide

This makes the internal IT team’s work much easier.

6. Annual inspections: Maintenance & Health Check

AITS offers:

  • Cable condition inspections
  • Firmware updates
  • Log reviews
  • Configuration backups
  • Equipment temperature and status checks

to support reliable operation 24/7.

AITS professionalism that customers can see

  • Names and tags on every cable and device for easier future maintenance
  • Engineers working to international standards, including TIA and ISO
  • Complete network documentation at enterprise level
  • On-site troubleshooting several times faster than before

body:
The 2000s marked the period when the termInternet of Things (IoT)was defined and gained acceptance. Smart homes expanded beyond local control to connectdevices to the internet.

🔧Technical Deep Insight

1. The origins of the term IoT

• In 1999, Kevin Ashton used the term“Internet of Things”to describe internet-connected RFID and sensor systems

• The concept was quickly applied tosmart homesacross the industry

2. Protocols & Standards

• Wi-Fi (802.11b/g)became widespread in homes

• Specialized IoT protocols such asZigbee (2002), Z-Wave (2004)were developed for low-power devices

• Systems began supportingWireless Mesh Networksfor large numbers of devices

3. Mobile Integration

• Early smartphones such as BlackBerry and iPhone (2007) enabled app-based home device control

• Applications began supportingremote control of lighting, air conditioning and security systems

🏠Laying the foundations of smart homes

• Network Layer:From LAN to internet and wireless mesh

• Device Layer:From a few devices to interconnected sensors, cameras, lighting and HVAC

• User Layer:From remotes and PCs to smartphones and the internet

The Internet of Things Concept (2000s): When Everything Became Connected

The 2000s were defined by a new paradigm: the Internet of Things (IoT). Instead of thinking of automation as isolated systems, the vision became one where every device could connect to the internet, share data, and be controlled remotely.

🔧 Technical Deep Insight

1. The Birth of the Term “IoT”

• In 1999, Kevin Ashton coined the term “Internet of Things” to describe RFID and sensor systems connected to the internet.

• This idea quickly expanded into the smart home sector.

2. Protocols and Standards

• Wi-Fi (802.11b/g) adoption surged in homes, enabling wireless device connectivity.

• Specialized IoT protocols such as Zigbee (2002) and Z-Wave (2004) emerged to support low-power, low-bandwidth devices.

• Wireless mesh networks allowed multiple devices to interconnect seamlessly.

3. Mobile Integration

• The rise of smartphones (BlackBerry, iPhone 2007) brought mobile apps that could control home devices.

• Users could now manage lights, HVAC, and security systems remotely via the internet.

The PC and Networking Era (1990s): When Homes Went Digital

The 1990s marked a critical transition: smart homes shifted from exclusive, luxury systems to digitally connected environments powered by personal computers and local networks.

🔧 Technical Deep Insight

1. PC-Based Control

• Early home automation software ran on Windows or DOS PCs, connected via RS-232 serial ports and parallel ports.

• Users could create schedules and macros — for example, automating lights, appliances, or sprinkler systems.

2. Local Area Networks (LANs)

• Homes began adopting Ethernet (10BASE-T) and Token Ring to connect devices.

• The concept of a home server emerged, acting as a hub to send commands across the system.

• Multi-room audio and entertainment systems started to integrate with LANs.

3. Early Remote Access

• Dial-up modems (14.4–56 kbps) allowed remote control from outside the home.

• Users could dial into their system to switch lights on/off or arm security remotely.

• This was the first real-world implementation of the IoT concept — remote connectivity for home devices.

🏠 Foundations for Smart Homes

• Digital Layer: Transition from mechanical/relay logic → software-driven automation.

• Networking Layer: LANs inside the home created the backbone for future IoT ecosystems.

• Remote Access: Dial-up control paved the way for cloud and smartphone-based smart home management we rely on today.

X10 (1975): The First Smart Home Communication Protocol

In 1975, Scottish company Pico Electronics introduced X10, the first protocol that allowed household devices to communicate with each other using existing power lines. This breakthrough marked the beginning of networked smart homes.

🔧 Technical Deep Insight

1. Communication Method

• X10 transmitted digital data packets at 120 kHz over standard 110V/220V electrical wiring.

• Each signal carried a House Code (A–P) and a Unit Code (1–16), allowing control of up to 256 devices.

2. Operation

• Receiver modules, such as lamp dimmers or plug-in switches, could be turned on/off or dimmed based on commands sent from a central controller.

• X10 was unidirectional — commands were sent, but devices could not send status updates back.

3. Technical Limitations

• No feedback mechanism meant users couldn’t confirm if a command succeeded.

• Vulnerable to electrical noise from motors or other appliances.

• Very low speed (~20 bits/s), supporting only basic functions.

🏠 Foundation for Smart Homes

• Network Layer: Moved from centralized push-button systems to true device-to-device communication.

• Scalability: Allowed many devices to coexist under one control system.

• Standardization: X10 became the global home automation standard for more than 20 years, widely used until the 1990s.

Before the term smart home existed, the early twentieth century introduced the world tohousehold electrical appliances.Inventions such aselectric refrigerators, washing machines and vacuum cleanerstransformed daily life. Though homes were not internet-connected, these werethe first steps toward home automation.

Early electric refrigerators usedthe vapor compression refrigeration cyclewith compressors and electromechanical thermostats to maintain a stable temperature. This environmental control developed toward today’sSmart HVACsystems

Electric washing machines of the period useduniversal motorsand washing programs controlled byelectromechanical timers.These principles laid the foundations forProgrammable Logic Control (PLC)seen in modern smart appliances.

Meanwhile, vacuum cleaners usedseries-wound motorsto create strong suction. Cloth bag filtration evolved intoCyclone Separationand later intoHEPA Filterwith filtration concepts developing toward air quality monitoring in today’s smart homes.

We can see thatsmart homes developed gradually: human labor → machinery → electricity → automation.These changes laid the foundations of the smart homes we use today.

The Birth of Electrical Convenience: The First Step Toward Smart Homes (1900s–1930s)

Long before the term Smart Home was coined, the early 20th century marked a quiet revolution in how people lived. For the first time, electric household appliances replaced manual labor and purely mechanical devices. Innovations such as the electric refrigerator, washing machine, and vacuum cleaner didn’t just save time—they redefined what it meant for a home to be “modern.”

The electric refrigerator worked on the vapor compression cycle, using a compressor, condenser, and evaporator to control temperature. Regulation came through a simple electromechanical thermostat, which was essentially the earliest form of automated environmental control—a direct ancestor of today’s smart HVAC systems.

Washing machines of the era relied on universal motors (capable of running on both AC and DC) and were programmed with electromechanical timers. These mechanical timers may look primitive now, but they introduced the concept of “programmed cycles,” laying the groundwork for programmable control systems we see in modern smart appliances.

Meanwhile, vacuum cleaners used series-wound motors to generate powerful suction. Their filter systems evolved from simple cloth bags to cyclonic separation, and eventually HEPA filters. This same principle of monitoring and controlling air quality is central to smart environmental sensors today.

From these innovations, we can see the clear trajectory: manual effort → mechanization → electrification → automation. These first steps of electrical convenience may not have been “smart” by name, but they created the foundation for the fully connected smart homes we now enjoy.

title: CCTV installation checklist: what should you prepare?
description: CCTV installation needs planning. This checklist covers camera quantity and type, positioning around entrances, fences and parking for complete coverage, and storage and cabling choices. IP cameras provide sharper images with LAN/Wi-Fi connectivity and online viewing; analog cameras cost less and suit existing systems. The article recommends IP cameras for phone viewing, at least 1080p Full HD for day and night, and 4MP–8MP for larger areas or details such as plates. Cat6 LAN cabling supports IP camera speed and reliability…
body:
CCTV installation requires careful planning beyond purchasing and mounting cameras. Many people ask how many cameras they need?or which type to choose?This checklist helps cover the important steps.

  1. Should camera locations be planned first?

Yes. Plan around risk points such as entrances, exits, fences, parking and surrounding areas. Good positioning provides coverage with fewer cameras.

  1. Which cameras should you choose: IP or analog?

• IP Camera– Sharper images, LAN or Wi-Fi connectivity and online viewing

• Analog Camera– Lower cost and suited to existing systems

For mobile viewing, the article recommends IP cameras.

  1. What resolution is needed?

At least1080p (Full HD)for clear daytime and nighttime images. Large areas or small details such as license plates may need 4MP–8MP.

  1. How should cables and infrastructure be managed?

• UsesCat6 LAN cablesfor IP cameras, supporting speed and stability

• Route cables through conduits to prevent damage

• Keep LAN cable runs within 100 meters per connection

  1. Which recorder should you choose: NVR or DVR?

• NVR– For IP cameras, with PoE providing power and data over one cable

• DVR– For analog cameras using coaxial cables

Tip: choose a recorder with at least 2–4 spare channels for future expansion.

  1. How much storage is needed?

It depends on camera count, resolution and retention time. For example, eight 1080p cameras recording for 15 days may need a 4TB–6TB hard drive.

  1. Should you hire an installer or do it yourself?

For neat installation and reliability, use professionals who can plan power, route cables, configure systems and test recording thoroughly.

Yes — plan in advance based on risk areas such as entrances, fences, garages, and perimeters. Proper planning covers blind spots and reduces the total number of cameras needed.

  1. Which Type Should I Choose: IP or Analog?

• IP Camera – Higher resolution, connects via LAN/Wi-Fi, supports online viewing.

• Analog Camera – Lower cost, good for existing analog systems.

FAQ inside: For mobile viewing, IP Camera is recommended.

  1. What Resolution Should I Use?

At least 1080p (Full HD) for clear day and night footage. For wide areas or small details (like license plates), use 4MP–8MP.

  1. How Should I Manage Cabling?

• Use Cat6 LAN cable for IP Cameras to ensure speed and stability.

• Protect cables in conduits.

• Keep cable length under 100 meters per run (for LAN).

  1. Which Recorder Should I Use (NVR/DVR)?

• NVR – For IP Cameras, supports PoE for single-cable power and data.

• DVR – For Analog Cameras, uses coaxial cable.

Tip: Choose a recorder with at least 2–4 extra channels for future expansion.

  1. How Much Storage Do I Need?

Depends on camera count, resolution, and retention days. Example: 8 cameras at 1080p for 15 days may require a 4TB–6TB HDD.
